cards.lead: City-wide water-carried sewerage in Hamburg and London
cards.note: The ICE source credits William Lindley's Hamburg sewers with over 11 km built in the three years after the May 1842 fire, and says his plans were influenced by Edwin Chadwick, so the origin is derived rather than independent. London's Bazalgette main drainage (1859 to 1875, Museum of London) is a separate achievement and is not covered by this card; a separate record is needed.
cards.name: Planned underground sewer network, Hamburg
cards.summary: After the 1842 fire, William Lindley designed underground sewers for Hamburg, among the first planned sewer systems in mainland Europe.
cards.description: After the fire of 5 May 1842, William Lindley helped plan the rebuilding of Hamburg and oversaw the construction of underground sewers. The ICE says his plans were influenced by the English reformer Edwin Chadwick, and that more than 11 km of sewers were built in the following three years.
cards.origin_note: The ICE source says Lindley's plans were influenced by Edwin Chadwick, an English reformer, which is evidenced transmission of sanitary ideas.

impact.note: Lindley's designs made a difference in other German towns and mainland European cities (ICE), so reach is lowered from the lead's 3 to 2 because the sources show a regional spread, not most of humanity.

cards.why: The fire left about a third of Hamburg's streets in ruins, and the reconstruction gave Lindley an opportunity to modernise the city.

events.label: from 1842
events.statement: After the 1842 fire, Lindley designed and oversaw the first underground sewers in mainland Europe.
events.quote: His plans – influenced by the English social reformer Edwin Chadwick – saw him design and oversee the construction of the first underground sewers in mainland Europe.

events.label: 1842 to 1845
events.statement: More than 11 km of underground sewers were built in Hamburg in the three years after the May 1842 fire.
events.quote: More than 11km were built in the following three years.

sources.title: Hamburg: A City Transformed by Civil Engineering

open_questions: Settle the start date: this source gives 1842 to 1845, while other pages give 1843 or 1848 without a checked source.
London's Bazalgette main drainage (1859 to 1875, Museum of London) is not covered here; it needs its own card, with the London Museum sentence 'His solution, completed in 1875' as its base.

cards.note: The lead's Teotihuacan figures (about 100,000 people, a grid plan) belong to a much later city and were not checked here. The best-sourced case in this window is Monte Albán, founded around 500 BCE, where urban residents were not primarily farmers; the origin is unknown because the source does not say whether it was independent.
cards.name: Monte Albán, a hilltop city in the Valley of Oaxaca
cards.summary: Monte Albán, founded around 500 BCE on a hilltop in the Valley of Oaxaca, became a city whose residents were not primarily farmers.
cards.description: Around 500 BCE a new hilltop centre, Monte Albán, was established where the valley's three arms meet, on land where farming was riskier than on the valley floor. Its urban residents were not primarily farmers, and rural surpluses alone were unlikely to feed them all.
cards.origin_note: The source describes the founding of Monte Albán but does not say whether it was independent of other Mesoamerican cities.

impact.note: The source shows a city serving one valley, not spread across Mesoamerica, so reach is lowered from 2 to 1; depth is lowered to 2 because the source does not show a change in the basis of life across the region.

events.label: c. 500 BCE
events.statement: Monte Albán was established as a new hilltop centre around 500 BCE.
events.quote: Around 500 BCE, a new hilltop center, Monte Albán, was established at the nexus of the valley’s three arms

sources.title: The Foundation of Monte Albán, Intensification, and Growth: Coactive Processes and Joint Production

open_questions: Establish the population of Monte Albán in its early centuries; this source gives no figure.
Check whether San Lorenzo (c. 1200 BCE) counts as urban, and record Teotihuacan (a grid-planned city) as its own card.

cards.lead: Mammoth-bone dwellings on the East European Plain
cards.note: The dated Mezhyrich structures are about 18,000 years old, within the lead's range but well below its 25,000 claim for early built dwellings. The first-known claim rests on comparison with Kostenki 11 and Ohalo II, which I could not check before the search limit was reached, so origin stays unknown.
cards.name: Mammoth-bone structures at Mezhyrich
cards.summary: Hunters in present-day Ukraine built structures almost entirely from mammoth bones, the largest dated to about 18,000 years ago.
cards.description: Hunter-gatherers in present-day Ukraine built structures made almost entirely of mammoth bones. The largest dates to 18,248 to 17,764 years ago, and the occupation was short, possibly a single or a few visits over centuries.
cards.origin_note: The source dates the Mezhyrich structures but makes no comparison with other sites, so it cannot show whether they were independent.

impact.note: Scores kept from the lead: the structures are a region's worth of evidence, and the depth reflects a new kind of built shelter, though the source calls them practical shelters rather than permanent homes.

cards.why: Trees were scarce and winters brutal, so people built with mammoth bones.

events.label: 18,248 to 17,764 years ago
events.statement: Dated remains show the largest Mezhyrich structure was built 18,248 to 17,764 years before present, which is about 16,300 to 15,800 BCE (converted by subtracting from 1950).
events.quote: The largest structure at Mezhyrich dates to 18,248–17,764 years ago, during the harshest phase of the last Ice Age.

sources.title: Ice age architecture: how mammoth bones reveal human ingenuity

open_questions: Search for and fetch the Kostenki 11 mammoth-bone structure dating (Pryor 2020) and the Ohalo II brush huts before any first-known claim is made.
Fetch the primary 2025 article by Chu, Shydlovskyi and Maier (Open Research Europe); this card rests on the Leiden summary. The coordinates come from a reference page, not a cited source.

cards.lead: Industrialised large-panel housing in France and the Soviet Union
cards.note: The 1948 patent is confirmed by Solopova (2025). The same article says the Camus panel was produced in his factories from 1954, which conflicts with the 1950 production start in its abstract, and I found no source for the claim that several hundred million people were rehoused.
cards.name: Camus prefabricated concrete panel housing, Le Havre
cards.summary: Raymond Camus's factory-cast concrete panels built housing at Le Havre from 1949, and an export contract to the USSR was signed by 1956.
cards.description: Engineer Raymond Camus cast large concrete panels in a disused warehouse at Le Havre from 1950, and built 10 apartment buildings and 65 detached houses between 1949 and 1953. By 1956 he had signed a contract to export the system to the USSR, and the Soviet 1957 housing decree set commitments for millions of square metres of new living space.
cards.origin_note: The sources record Camus's patent, system and export contract but do not say whether he devised the method without knowledge of earlier large-panel work.

impact.note: The sources show one French region and an export contract, so reach is lowered from the lead's 2 to 1; depth stays at 1 as a cheaper, faster form of building.

events.label: June 1948
events.statement: Raymond Camus registered a patent for prefabricated apartment blocks in June 1948.
events.quote: In June 1948, Raymond Camus registered a patent for the construction of prefabricated apartment blocks.

events.label: 1949 to 1953
events.statement: Camus built 10 apartment buildings and 65 detached houses with the system between 1949 and 1953.
events.quote: Between 1949 and 1953, Camus constructed 10 apartment buildings and 65 detached houses, employing his heavy prefabrication system.

events.statement: Camus began producing concrete panels in an abandoned warehouse at Le Havre in 1950.
events.quote: In 1950, he initiated the production of concrete panels in an abandoned warehouse at the port of Le Havre.

events.label: by 1956

events.quote: By 1956, he signed a contract to export his heavy prefabrication system to the USSR

events.quote: the decree of 1957 set commitments in the millions for new square meters of living space

cards.lead: Monumental stone enclosures in Upper Mesopotamia
cards.name: Monumental enclosures at Göbekli Tepe
cards.summary: Hunter-gatherers at Göbekli Tepe, southeastern Anatolia, built large curvilinear stone enclosures in the Pre-Pottery Neolithic A, with no domesticated plants or animals found.
cards.description: Layer III at Göbekli Tepe, assigned to the Pre-Pottery Neolithic A, has large curvilinear enclosures. The excavator suggested the early layers were built and used by hunter-gatherers, and the enclosures were later backfilled in what has been interpreted as an intentional burial.
cards.origin_note: The source dates the earliest monumental architecture to the tenth and ninth millennia cal. BC and names no earlier monumental construction, but it does not say the enclosures were the first known, so the origin is not established.

impact.note: Scores kept from the lead: one site is evidenced and the sources do not show spread, but the lead's scores are not contradicted.

events.label: tenth and ninth millennia cal. BC
events.statement: Megalithic architecture at Göbekli Tepe is dated to the tenth and ninth millennia cal. BC, which includes the lead's c. 9500 BCE.
events.quote: Excavations carried out in different areas of the site yielded megalithic architecture dated to the twelfth and eleventh millennia cal. BP (tenth and ninth millennia cal. BC: Schmidt 2010).

sources.title: Geometry and architectural planning at Göbekli Tepe, Turkey

open_questions: Check the radiocarbon dates of Enclosure D (about 9984 ± 42 BP, Dietrich and Schmidt) from a fetched primary source; the card does not rely on them.
Establish whether the pillars were quarried and multi-tonne, and whether the builders were settled; the card does not rely on either.
